## Overview

**Cambodia Land Price Analysis and Prediction** — part of the [Data Science Projects Collection](https://github.com/PaulChanCyber/Data-Science-Project-). ITC Group 3 capstone: scrape land listings, EDA, and best-model selection for Cambodian land prices.

## Background of the Study

This study examines **Cambodian land and property markets across provinces** in Cambodia—a context where digital classifieds and e-commerce listings have accelerated price transparency but not necessarily price *understanding*. Stakeholders include buyers, sellers, and small investors comparing plot prices. **Group 3 — Land Price Analysis** (ITC AMS, PDS 2022–2023, Lecturer CHAN Sophal). Five-member team capstone on Cambodian land listings. The project folder on GitHub contains notebooks, and in many cases a formal **Project Guideline** PDF that records the instructor-approved objectives, timeline, and evaluation plan. That document is the contract between the student team and the course: it states what will be delivered, which algorithms will be compared, and how success will be measured. The work was completed in the **Programming for Data Science (PDS)** course at the **Institute of Technology of Cambodia (ITC)**, Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, under instructor **CHAN Sophal**. Deliverables typically include a **Project Guideline** alignment document, Jupyter notebooks, visualizations, a written report, and presentation slides—mirroring how data analysts are expected to document real engagements for technical and non-technical audiences.

## Motivation of the Study

**Why this topic matters:** Land remains a core asset class; without models, buyers rely on anecdotal comparables that ignore size, road access, and district effects. Land is a primary store of wealth in Cambodia; buyers and planners need defensible comparables across provinces where listing quality and units vary widely. From an academic standpoint, **Cambodia Land Price Analysis and Prediction** trains competencies employers list repeatedly: pandas data wrangling, visualization literacy, scikit-learn modeling, and clear written communication. From a practical standpoint, even a simple benchmark model helps buyers, sellers, and small investors comparing plot prices negotiate fairer deals and spot overpriced listings. The motivation is therefore both **social** (fairer, more informed transactions) and **pedagogical** (evidence that the team followed the guideline, compared models fairly, and can explain limitations such as sample bias, missing data, and temporal drift).

## Project Guidelines & Objectives

The following objectives and steps are taken from the team's **Project Guideline** (see GitHub) and reflect how the instructor graded the capstone: **From *Final Project Guideline Land Price Analysis*:**

1. **Define problem & goal** — state the analytical problem; goal: find the **best model for land price analysis**
2. **Data collection** — web scraping from sites with land listing information
3. **EDA** — cleaning, preprocessing, visualization
4. **Modeling & analysis** — train/compare predictive models
5. **Conclusion** — summarize findings and model choice Teams were expected to show intermediate artifacts—not only a final accuracy number. That includes data dictionaries, plots defending modeling choices, and a short conclusion on which model to deploy or recommend for the stated business question.

## Data Collection & Preparation

Reliable conclusions depend on documenting **where data came from**, **how often it was collected**, and **what each column means**. For this project: Scraped land listings from Cambodian property websites; features include location, area, and listing attributes (see project notebooks). Typical preparation steps across PDS scraping projects include deduplicating listings, standardizing currencies (USD vs. KHR), parsing text fields (e.g., '3+ bedrooms'), handling missing values with explicit rules, and flagging extreme prices before modeling. Those steps reduce leakage and prevent a single erroneous row from dominating metrics.

## Methodology & Analysis

Analytical work proceeded in reproducible notebook stages so instructors could rerun cells during defense sessions: Standard PDS pipeline: clean scraped text/numeric fields, visualize price distributions by region, engineer location and parcel features, fit regression models, compare errors. Where applicable, teams compared multiple algorithms rather than reporting a single default model. Feature engineering was justified with plots (distributions, correlations, geographic breakdowns) so stakeholders could see *why* variables entered the model—not only *that* they improved error metrics.

## Model Evaluation

Model evaluation followed train/validation/test discipline taught in PDS: Model comparison on test split; emphasis on **best predictive model** per guideline goal. Beyond scalar error, teams were encouraged to inspect **residuals** (regression), **confusion matrices** (classification), or **forecast overlays** (time series) to detect systematic bias—such as underpricing premium districts or overfitting rare categories.

## Results & Key Learnings

Regional land price insights and a documented modeling benchmark for ITC PDS assessment. Completing **Cambodia Land Price Analysis and Prediction** provides evidence of end-to-end data science execution: from raw scrape to defended conclusions. For portfolio readers, the GitHub repository contains the artifacts to verify claims—notebooks, and in many folders, slide decks and PDF reports. Limitations are worth stating explicitly: scraped data snapshots age quickly; models trained in 2022–2023 may need retraining as market conditions shift. That honesty is part of professional practice.
